column3: It gives the sacrificial setting: animals provided by God are named over in worship of the one God.
Its call to taqwa supports the focus's claim that protective devotion, rather than material offering, matters.
Reaching moral good through giving what one loves loosely parallels the focus's distinction between an act's material and moral value.
It exactly joins magnifying God with the guidance He has given, the focus's stated purpose for the subjected animals.
It directly says the value of God's ritual markers is taqwa in hearts, anticipating the focus's contrast.
It connects taqwa with enduring reward, but lacks the focus's sacrificial-material contrast.
Its expiation rules make intention and accountable action relevant, but do not address sacrifice or taqwa as what reaches God.
It offers the nearby promise of generous provision and forgiveness without explaining the focus's ritual criterion.
Its account of lost guidance only broadly contrasts with the focus's grateful response to divine guidance.
It frames Hajj through restraint and names taqwa as its best provision, closely matching the focus's Hajj setting.
The prey comes within human reach as an unseen test of reverence, a pointed parallel to the focus's language of what reaches.
Guidance and glad tidings recur, but this brief formula adds no sacrificial or taqwa-specific relation.
The reward of doers of good only broadly corresponds to the focus's closing glad tidings for the muhsinin.
It continues the nearby account of sacrificial animals, their benefits, and their appointed destination at the ancient House.
It describes God guiding followers to paths of peace, supporting the focus's response of magnifying Him for guidance.
It names blood, flesh, and slaughter for other than God in dietary law, furnishing a related material-and-devotional boundary.
It supplies the Hajj summons that establishes the ritual setting of the focus passage.
It calls the revelation a reminder for the God-conscious, reinforcing taqwa as an active receptive orientation.
Its repeated dietary prohibition on blood, flesh, and non-divine dedication is materially close to the focus.
It joins taqwa, patience, and the unfailing reward of the muhsinin, complementing the focus's final assurance.
God's exclusive greatness gives content to the focus's command to magnify Him.
The Hajj sequence commands remembrance of God because He guided the pilgrims, closely echoing the focus's final clause.
This nearby verse concerns proportionate retaliation and divine support, not sacrificial meaning or taqwa.
Its statement that opponents did not attain good only shares the reach vocabulary without the focus's moral contrast.
The formula about rewarding the muhsinin is a broad echo of the focus's closing phrase.
It presents gardens and rivers as the outcome for the God-conscious, extending the focus's taqwa theme.
The construction of Noah's ark and the mockery it receives do not clarify the sacrificial or devotional relation.
Its reward formula for the muhsinin is a general, redundant parallel to the focus's ending.
It immediately defines the humble believers by reverent hearts, patience, prayer, and spending before the sacrifice sequence.
Fear of the Lord in the unseen and its reward gives a close general account of the taqwa named in the focus.
It makes taqwa the foundation of a worship space and pairs it with purification, though not sacrifice.
The verse concerns frustrated hostility toward divine aid rather than the meaning of sacrificial animals.
It uses the same divine subjection formula for created things made available to people, clarifying the focus's sakhkhara relation.
Its glad tidings for believers loosely parallels the focus's closing command to give glad tidings.
The immediately preceding verse names the sacrificial animals, their food-sharing purpose, God's name, and their divinely subjected status.
Its restored flesh demonstrates divine power over bodily matter, but does not develop the focus's sacrificial contrast.
Its rewarded exertion and use of muhsinin give only a general resonance with the focus's closing commendation.
The punishment imagery of melting bodies and skins has no material connection to the sacrifice passage.
It explicitly classifies flowing blood, pork flesh, and slaughter for other than God, closely framing the focus's material terms.
It names taqwa within an ethical command, but does not relate it to worship, sacrifice, or what reaches God.
The deprivation of crops is a distant contrast to the focus's provided animal sustenance.
Mockery of the messenger does not clarify the focus's ritual or moral logic.
Its denial and reversal of who receives divine mercy shares reach language but concerns social judgment rather than sacrifice.
The destroyed towns and abandoned wells are unrelated to the focus's account of offering and taqwa.
Turning away in arrogance supplies no specific connection to sacrificial material or divine guidance.
The proclamation occurs on the greater pilgrimage and concerns dissociation from idolaters, offering only contextual Hajj resonance.
Its preservation of the reward of muhsinin is a general echo of the focus's final glad tidings.
Giving and taqwa are paired as a single righteous orientation, though no ritual offering is in view.
It explicitly names God as worthy of taqwa and forgiveness, directly supporting the focus's elevation of taqwa.
The terror of the Hour is in the same surah but does not illuminate the focus's sacrificial teaching.
The sun and moon are subjected to God on fixed courses, a cosmic counterpart to animals subjected for human use.
The garment of taqwa makes inward protective devotion better than outward covering, closely paralleling the focus's inward-over-material contrast.
The surah's closing call to worship, prayer, charity, and holding fast to God broadens the devotional response but not the sacrifice logic.
It identifies the God-conscious as recipients of gardens and bliss, extending the focus's taqwa theme.
The word of taqwa stabilizes believers against hostile pride, showing taqwa as a binding moral orientation.
Blood appears as a plague sign, a materially remote and adverse use of one of the focus's terms.
The revelation's warning that none is god but God culminates in a direct command to taqwa.
Its glad tidings for believers only repeats the focus's closing rhetorical form.
God protects the blessed from punishment, giving a concrete outcome to the protective sense of taqwa.
The prophetic call to taqwa is relevant but entirely general.
Its statement that God's covenant does not reach wrongdoers shares reach language but concerns leadership, not ritual value.
Chosen fruit in paradise does not clarify the focus's treatment of sacrifice or taqwa.
It pairs guidance with provision and later deviation, but remains distant from the focus's ritual claim.
Its dietary law explicitly treats carrion, blood, flesh, and slaughter not dedicated to God, directly adjacent to the focus's material categories.
Milk emerging from between refuse and blood in cattle highlights a divinely ordered transformation of animal material into provision.
The denial of guidance to defiantly disobedient people is only a general counterpoint to the focus's received guidance.
It joins divinely subjected creation, edible flesh, benefit, and gratitude, closely matching the focus's animal-use and thanks logic.
Desired flesh is granted as paradise provision, but it lacks the focus's distinction between flesh and taqwa.
Its command to fear God within a testimony procedure gives a distant ethical use of taqwa.
It says spending is not accepted from the defiantly disobedient, a meaningful contrast to the focus's concern with what reaches God.
Bird flesh as desired provision is materially adjacent but lacks sacrificial or devotional significance.
Security and guidance belong to faith unmingled with wrongdoing, a broad parallel to taqwa's protective orientation.
The household privacy rules do not connect to sacrifice, guidance, or taqwa in the focus.
Word distortion and disobedient speech have no specific relation to the focus's ritual criterion.
The repeated prophetic command to taqwa and obedience supports the focus's general devotional orientation.
It denies that submission is a human favor and attributes guidance to faith to God, sharpening the focus's gratitude for guidance.
Its command to share inheritance provision with relatives and the needy loosely echoes the sacrificial sharing around the focus.
The question about mocked people in Hell does not clarify the focus's sacrificial or moral distinction.
The wind is subjected for a measured outcome, providing a contrasting use of the same divine-subjection language.
Reward for every expenditure gives a loose relation to material acts receiving divine recompense.
It states within the surah that God guides whom He wills, supporting the focus's attribution of guidance to Him.
Calling Yusuf a muhsin offers only a general echo of the focus's final designation.
Its detailed animal-food restrictions relate to bodily material, but not to sacrifice or taqwa as what reaches God.
The repeated command to taqwa and obedience is relevant but general.
Revelation is a light through which God guides to a straight path, directly supporting the focus's response to guidance.
The absence of headache and intoxication in paradise is unrelated to the focus.
The direct command to magnify the Lord exactly supports the focus's purpose of magnifying God.
Discontent with divinely supplied food contrasts with the focus's thankful use of divinely subjected provision.
God's conclusive proof and power to guide all is a broad support for the focus's attribution of guidance to Him.
The Quran guides to what is most upright and gives glad tidings to righteous believers, echoing both focus clauses generally.
Book, judgment, prophethood, and good provision form a distant background for divinely given guidance and sustenance.
It calls voluntary forbearance nearer to taqwa, a general ethical instance rather than the focus's ritual teaching.
Its concern is concealed unbelief and distortion of judgment, not sacrifice, taqwa, or grateful guidance.
It links guidance from God with the lasting outcome of the home, supporting the focus's attribution of guidance to God.
Divine acceptance of repentance does not add a specific relation to the focus.
It contrasts those astray from God's path with the rightly guided, reinforcing the focus's emphasis on received guidance.
It affirms revealed truth while noting widespread unbelief, a broad counterpoint to grateful acceptance of guidance.
A community guides and acts justly by truth, extending divine guidance into communal conduct.
The prophetic command to taqwa and obedience supports the focus's devotional orientation without its sacrificial setting.
It gives gardens of bliss to the God-conscious, extending the focus's taqwa theme into its promised outcome.
It names the Safa and Marwah as God's ritual markers within Hajj, supplying the wider sanctuary-rite setting for the focus.
It commands completion of Hajj and Umrah for God and prescribes the accessible sacrificial offering when prevented.
After completing Hajj rites, pilgrims are commanded to remember God intensely, paralleling the focus's call to magnify Him.
It joins the appointed days of remembrance with taqwa at the close of pilgrimage observances.
It protects God's ritual markers, the sacred month, and marked sacrificial animals, directly framing their sanctity.
It states that God accepts only from the God-conscious, the clearest direct parallel to the focus's claim that taqwa, not animal matter, reaches Him.
Its Hajj expiation requires a livestock offering reaching the Ka'bah, closely connecting animal sacrifice, destination, and accountability.
It identifies the Ka'bah, sacred month, sacrificial animals, and garlands as God-established supports of the sanctuary order.
It commands eating what God's name was pronounced over, linking animal provision to conscious devotion to God.
It prohibits eating animals not named for God, making divine orientation rather than mere flesh decisive for consumption.
It condemns assigning shares of crops and livestock between God and alleged partners, a direct corrective to misconstrued offerings.
It explicitly dedicates prayer, sacrifice, life, and death wholly to God, giving the governing purpose of the focus's ritual act.
It commands eating God's lawful good provision and thanking Him, matching the focus's use of subjected animals in grateful worship.
It explicitly commands God's name over provided grazing livestock, then eating and feeding the poor, immediately completing the sacrifice-and-provision logic.
It continues the Hajj sequence through fulfillment of vows and circumambulation, providing the ritual frame around the focus.
It commands reverence for God's sanctities and avoidance of idolatry, supplying the devotional boundary for the sacrifice passage.
It affirms that every community has an appointed rite, extending the focus's teaching beyond one sacrificial instance.
The ransom of Ishmael with a great sacrifice supplies a major Qur'anic instance of an animal offering, though it does not state the focus's taqwa criterion.
It directly joins prayer to the Lord with sacrifice, expressing the God-directed intention that the focus makes explicit.
It permits what trained animals catch when God's name is mentioned and ends with taqwa, directly joining animal use, divine naming, and reverence.
It commands eating God's lawful good provision while fearing Him, a general counterpart to the focus's grateful use of animals.
It rejects invented consecrations of particular animals, clarifying that animal ritual status cannot be fabricated apart from God.
It criticizes fabricated restrictions on livestock and false claims about mentioning God's name over them, a direct distortion of the focus's devotional order.
It presents livestock as divinely created for human benefit, warmth, and food, providing the material-provision side of the focus.
It calls livestock a lesson and names drink, benefits, and food from them, extending the focus's account of animal provision.
It identifies livestock as a divine creation made available for human possession, introducing a close parallel to the focus's subjected animals.
It states that God subjected livestock so people may ride some and eat some, nearly restating the focus's provision logic.
It completes the livestock sequence with benefits, drink, and the question of gratitude, directly echoing the focus's thankful magnification.
It says God made livestock for people to ride and eat, a concise parallel to divinely ordered animal benefit.
It identifies livestock among the created means of travel, supporting the focus's broader language of divinely subjected creatures.
It commands remembrance and praise of the One who subjected transport, closely paralleling the focus's magnification after subjection.
